Title: Is Adversarial Robustness Ready for Prime Time? | by Andreas Maier | Medium
# **Is Adversarial Robustness Ready for Prime Time?**. ## **Introducing OODRobustBench for Distribution Shift**. Adversarial robustness — the capacity of a machine learning model to withstand carefully crafted attacks — has become a cornerstone of research in reliable artificial intelligence. For years, experts have focused on training algorithms to remain robust when tested on data that resemble what they saw during training. Datasets encountered in practice often differ drastically from those used for training, making it crucial to understand how models hold up against these shifts in input distribution. A new study titled “OODRobustBench: a Benchmark and Large-Scale Analysis of Adversarial Robustness under Distribution Shift” tackles precisely this question. It offers a timely reality check on whether today’s “robust” models can truly deliver when tested outside their comfort zone. This investigation is extremely relevant because distribution shifts happen all the time in real-world scenarios. ## Create an account to read the full story. results.title: Best Practices in Adversarial Defense and Robustness of AI Systems
results.content: # Best Practices in Adversarial Defense and Robustness of AI Systems. ### Dr. Sunando Roy. As artificial intelligence (AI) systems become more deeply embedded in critical applications, ensuring their robustness against adversarial attacks is of utmost importance. Adversarial attacks—including data poisoning, evasion techniques, and model extraction—pose serious threats to the integrity of AI, potentially leading to misclassifications, biased decisions, or even unauthorized duplication. Anomaly detection serves as a fundamental strategy in fortifying AI models. Adversarial Training for Model Resilience. Adversarial training enhances a model’s defenses by introducing adversarial examples during the learning phase. Robustness evaluations and simulations are essential to measure how well models respond to adversarial attacks. Using ensembles of AI models can significantly reduce susceptibility to adversarial and poisoning attacks by promoting diversity in decision-making. Evasion and transfer attacks involve manipulating inputs or using adversarial samples from related models. Cross-model testing with adversarial samples aids in understanding transferability vulnerabilities. * Adversarial Attack: Malicious attempts to manipulate AI systems through crafted inputs, poisoning, or extraction. * Model Ensemble: Combining multiple AI models to enhance resilience against attacks. * Data Poisoning: Introducing malicious data into training sets to compromise model performance. * Transfer Attack: Using adversarial samples effective on one model to attack a related model. * Backdoor and Tampering Detection: Validate backdoor detection protocols and model parameter audit reports for unauthorized changes. * Evasion and Transfer Attack Testing: Confirm evasion attack detection and transfer attack resilience through testing reports. * Model Extraction Defense: Assess model extraction testing protocols and knowledge transfer risk reports for vulnerabilities. * Third-Party Validation: Engage independent experts to review anomaly detection, adversarial training, and audit processes. * From Model Risk to AI Risk: Emerging Supervisory Perspectives on Governing Advanced Analytics. ### From Model Risk to AI Risk: Emerging Supervisory Perspectives on Governing Advanced Analytics. * ### Data Poisoning in the Wild: Risks, Realities, and the Urgent Need for Trustworthy AI. * ### Cybersecurity for AI Models: A Strategic Deep Dive into Model Inversion, Poisoning, and Trust Engineering. * ### Next-Gen AI Security: Protecting Sensitive Data During Model Training. * ### AI Model Vulnerability to Backdoors and the Role of Auditors in Model Validation.

results.title: OODRobustBench: a Benchmark of Adversarial Robustness under Distribution Shift
results.content: A benchmark for adversarial robustness under distribution shift. Existing works have made great progress in improving adversarial robustness, but typically test their method only on data from the same distribution as the training data, i.e. in-distribution (ID) testing. As a result, it is unclear how such robustness generalizes under input distribution shifts, i.e. out-of-distribution (OOD) testing. To address this issue we propose a benchmark named OODRobustBench to comprehensively assess OOD adversarial robustness using 23 dataset-wise shifts (i.e. naturalistic shifts in input distribution) and 6 threat-wise shifts (i.e., unforeseen adversarial threat models). CIFAR-10 (\( \ell\_\infty\)) CIFAR-10 (\( \ell\_2\)) ImageNet (\( \ell\_\infty\)). Leaderboard: CIFAR-10, \( \ell\_\infty = 8/255 \), untargeted attack. We use CIFAR-10.1, CIFAR-10.2, CINIC, and CIFAR-10-R (ImageNet-V2, ImagetNet-A, ImageNet-R, ObjectNet) to simulate input data distribution shift for the source datasets CIFAR-10 (ImageNet), while RobustBench only uses the latter source datasets. By contrast, our conclusion is derived from much more shifts on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet based on 706 models.
